entities.address: 4719-4727 S. Parkway (now Martin Luther King Drive), Chicago

claims.claim: Built by the National Theater Corporation for $1.5 million; opened February 4, 1928, as one of the first U.S. theaters built expressly to cater to the Black community.
claims.evidence: City of Chicago landmark report on the New Regal Theater states the Regal was 'built at 4719-27 South Parkway by the National Theater Corporation,' 'one of the first theaters in the country built expressly to cater to the black community,' 'constructed and furnished for $1.5 million,' and 'opened its doors on February 4, 1928.'
claims.source: City of Chicago, Commission on Chicago Historical and Architectural Landmarks, New Regal Theater designation report (February 1989)
claims.uncertainty: One popular blog gives February 24, 1928; the City's February 4 date is preferred. Seating capacity ~3,000 from secondary sources, not in the City report excerpt read.

claims.claim: The National Theater Corporation sold the Regal to the Balaban & Katz chain in 1931.
claims.evidence: City landmark report, ownership sequence.
claims.source: City of Chicago, New Regal Theater designation report (February 1989)

claims.claim: The Regal first came under Black ownership in 1961, when S. B. Fuller purchased it from the Englestein Company; Fuller lost it in 1968.
claims.evidence: City landmark report: 'the Regal came under black ownership for the first time in 1961 when S.B. Fuller purchased it from the Englestein Company,' losing it in 1968 to financial problems.
claims.source: City of Chicago, New Regal Theater designation report (February 1989)

claims.claim: The original Regal was demolished in 1973.
claims.evidence: City landmark report; corroborated by Encyclopedia of Chicago and preservation-history accounts.
claims.source: City of Chicago, New Regal Theater designation report (February 1989); Encyclopedia of Chicago

claims.claim: The Regal's architect is disputed: attributions to Levy and Klein, Edward Eichenbaum, and John Eberson all circulate. Eberson definitively designed the Avalon (New Regal) at 79th Street — likely the source of confusion.
claims.evidence: Track A survey: Wikipedia current text credits Levy and Klein; an earlier Wikipedia version credited Edward Eichenbaum; a Black-history site credits John Eberson; Track B survey repeats the Eichenbaum attribution.
claims.source: Track A compilation of secondary sources (2026-09-28)
claims.uncertainty: Do not publish an architect attribution without permit or trade-press verification.

claims.claim: The claim that the Regal 'predated the Apollo Theater' is imprecise as commonly written.
claims.evidence: The Apollo building opened 1913-14; it became a Black venue in 1934, after the Regal (1928). True only with the qualifier 'as a Black entertainment venue.'
claims.source: Track F red-team note, citing City of Chicago landmark report

entities.name: Regal Theater (original)
entities.summary: Premier Black-audience theater of the South Side, built expressly for Black audiences by the white-owned National Theater Corporation. Not Black-owned until S. B. Fuller purchased it in 1961.

entities.address: 4733 S. Parkway (now Martin Luther King Drive), Chicago

claims.claim: Opened November 1927 at 4733 S. Parkway; accommodated more than 4,000; demolished in the early 1970s.
claims.evidence: Jazz Age Chicago research blog and Bo Lindstrom's venue compilation converge on 4733 S. Parkway, November 1927 opening, 4,000+ capacity, and early-1970s demolition.
claims.source: Jazz Age Chicago (blog); Bo Lindstrom, 'Chicago South Side Clubs and Venues c. 1915-1930' (2012)
claims.uncertainty: Capacity and demolition details rest on enthusiast/compilation sources; corridor-level demolition of the 47th/S. Parkway complex in 1972-73 corroborates timing.

claims.claim: Closing year is disputed: 1948 (UChicago Library jazz exhibit) vs. 1954 (Jazz Age Chicago; Lindstrom compilation).
claims.evidence: UChicago Library exhibit: 'a major jazz center from 1928 until 1948.' Jazz Age Chicago and Lindstrom: closed 1954.
claims.source: UChicago Library exhibition text (1996-97); Jazz Age Chicago; Lindstrom (2012)
claims.uncertainty: Defender entertainment pages or city directories should settle this.

claims.claim: Part of a single commercial complex with the Regal Theater and South Center Department Store, developed by the Englestein syndicate.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago states the Regal was 'part of a larger construction project that included the Savoy Ballroom and the South Center department store.'
claims.uncertainty: The Englestein brothers' exact corporate vehicle and I. Jay Faggen's operating role rest on single secondary sources (Provisional).

entities.name: Savoy Ballroom (Chicago)
entities.summary: Large South Side ballroom anchoring the 47th/South Parkway 'bright-light district'; part of the Englestein-developed Regal/Savoy/South Center complex.

claims.claim: The South Center Department Store was part of the Regal/Savoy commercial complex developed by the Englestein syndicate.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago: the Regal was 'part of a larger construction project that included the Savoy Ballroom and the South Center department store.'
claims.uncertainty: Open/close dates, ownership, and demolition fate all unresolved.

entities.name: South Center Department Store
entities.summary: Department store in the Englestein-developed 47th/S. Parkway complex. Open/close dates, ownership, and fate unresolved.

claims.claim: Opened circa 1917; operated into about 1930; demolished 1972, leaving an empty parking lot.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation (ca. 1917-30); MAS Context preservation journalism (opened 1917, demolished 1972).
claims.uncertainty: Exact open/close years approximate; ownership not verified.

entities.name: Metropolitan Theater (Ascher's Metropolitan)
entities.summary: Early Black-audience theater on the South Parkway corridor, demolished a year before the Regal.

claims.claim: Building constructed 1909 as an auto garage; converted to a dance hall and opened August 3, 1921, as the Sunset Cafe; owned by Ed Fox and Sam Rifas, managed by Joe Glaser, with Carroll Dickerson's band.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation: 'Built in 1909 as a garage and converted to a dancehall 1921. Open Aug 3, 1921... Owners: Ed Fox and Sam Rifas; Joe Glaser, manager... Carroll Dickerson.'
claims.uncertainty: Single compilation source; operator/manager details need Defender/directory corroboration.

claims.claim: An integrated 'Black and Tan' club that hosted Louis Armstrong (1926), Earl Hines (from 1928), and Cab Calloway.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation; UChicago Library jazz-exhibit text places the Sunset within the South Side jazz-club ecology.
claims.source: Bo Lindstrom (2012); UChicago Library exhibition text (1996-97)
claims.uncertainty: Exact performer tenure years (e.g., Hines 1928-35) overlap with his known Grand Terrace residency; treat years as shaky.

claims.claim: Renamed the New Sunset Cafe in October 1932; later housed Meyers Ace Hardware (from the 1960s), whose proprietors preserved the original jazz murals; the hardware store closed in February 2017; the building stands as a Chicago Landmark (designated 1998).
claims.evidence: Lindstrom (renaming); Medill Reports Chicago on the February 2017 hardware-store closure; City of Chicago landmark address list.
claims.source: Bo Lindstrom (2012); Medill Reports Chicago (~2017); City of Chicago landmark list
claims.uncertainty: Current occupant and mural-preservation status after 2017 unresolved.

claims.claim: Closure date disputed: 1937 (Lindstrom) vs. operation through the 1940s with closure in 1950 (current business site, weak).
claims.evidence: Lindstrom: 'Open Aug 3, 1921-1937.' The current business site claims operation through the 1940s and closure in 1950.
claims.uncertainty: Defender entertainment listings should resolve.

claims.claim: The Sunset Cafe is a separate venue from the Grand Terrace Cafe at 3955 S. Parkway; claims that 'the Sunset Cafe, also known as The Grand Terrace Cafe' are a conflation error.
claims.evidence: Distinct addresses (315-317 E. 35th vs. 3955 S. Parkway); Lindstrom documents the Grand Terrace as a separate venue.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit remediation 2026-09-28: downgraded Verified -> Provisional and flagged weak_source_only. Source rests solely on weak/laundered sources (Bo Lindstrom (2012)); queued for re-sourcing before any public use.

entities.name: Sunset Cafe (later New Sunset Cafe)
entities.summary: Landmarked integrated ('Black and Tan') jazz club in a converted 1909 auto garage; hosted Louis Armstrong, Earl Hines, and Cab Calloway. Distinct venue from the Grand Terrace Cafe despite frequent online conflation.

claims.claim: The Grand Terrace Cafe operated until 1928 in the same building as the Grand Terrace Ballroom (aka Peerless Theater); the ballroom opened 1917 as the Grand Oak Theatre, became the Peerless Theater later that year, closed until 1937 when it opened as the Park Theatre, closed 1958, and reopened as the Ritz Theatre 1964-65.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation entries for the Grand Terrace Cafe and Grand Terrace Ballroom.
claims.uncertainty: Single source; current/final fate unresolved.

entities.name: Grand Terrace Cafe / Grand Terrace Ballroom
entities.summary: Venue at 3955 S. Parkway; the Grand Terrace Cafe operated until 1928; the building cycled through Grand Oak Theatre, Peerless Theater, Park Theatre, and Ritz Theatre identities.

entities.address: 3520 S. State Street per UChicago (1914); 3618 S. State Street per NPS nomination

claims.claim: The Dreamland Cafe was a pioneering South Side jazz venue that opened in 1914, associated with King Oliver, Baby Dodds, Honore Dutrey, Alberta Hunter, and Lil Hardin Armstrong's Dreamland Syncopators featuring Louis Armstrong on cornet.
claims.evidence: UChicago Library exhibition text drawing on the Chicago Jazz Archive describes the 'grand Dreamland Cafe, opened at 3520 South State Street in 1914' and its performers.
claims.source: UChicago Library, 'From Dreamland to Showcase: Jazz in Chicago, 1912 to 1996' (exhibition text, 1996-97)
claims.uncertainty: Performers standard accounts; specific dates provisional.

claims.claim: Address is disputed: the UChicago exhibit gives 3520 S. State; the NPS Black Metropolis nomination lists the Dreamland Cafe at 3618 S. State. No source states a relocation.
claims.evidence: Direct conflict between the two sources.
claims.source: UChicago Library exhibition text (1996-97); NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985)
claims.uncertainty: City directories 1914-1925 should resolve; ownership also unresolved.

claims.claim: Paddy Harmon's Dreamland Ballroom (Paulina and Van Buren, near West Side) is a distinct venue and a documented source of confusion.
claims.evidence: Track A survey.

entities.name: Dreamland Cafe
entities.summary: Pioneering South Side jazz venue; address disputed between 3520 and 3618 S. State; associated with King Oliver, Lil Hardin Armstrong's Dreamland Syncopators, and Louis Armstrong.

claims.claim: Robert T. Motts's Pekin Theatre at 2700 S. State was the first Black-owned musical/vaudeville stock theater in the United States; both Black and white audiences were admitted; it reopened as a dance hall in 1918.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; Illinois Humanities; NPS nomination places Motts's theater at 2700 S. State as an early catalyst for later music venues; Lindstrom describes the dance-hall conversion.
claims.source: Illinois Humanities; NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985); Bo Lindstrom (2012)
claims.uncertainty: Motts's death in 1911 needs verification.

claims.claim: Opening year is reported as 1904 (theater opening) vs. June 18, 1905 (first all-Black show); demolition in 1946 rests on weak sourcing only.
claims.evidence: Track A survey of secondary sources.
claims.uncertainty: Likely 1904 opening vs. June 18, 1905 first all-Black production; needs trade-press verification.

entities.name: Pekin Theatre
entities.summary: Robert T. Motts's theater, widely cited as the first Black-owned stock theater in the United States, admitting both Black and white audiences; reopened as a dance hall in 1918.

claims.claim: Ownership in 1918 is listed as Louis B. Anderson, William Bottoms, and Virgil Williams; in 1921 it became Lincoln Gardens under owner Florence Majors; King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band played there 1923-24; it caught fire Christmas Eve 1924 and closed 1925-26, becoming the New Charleston Cafe in 1927 and later the Cafe de Paris.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation entry; the NPS nomination also lists Royal/Lincoln Gardens at 459 E. 31st without ownership detail.
claims.source: Bo Lindstrom (2012); NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985)
claims.uncertainty: Ownership, fire, and Cafe de Paris sequence all rest on one compilation; Alderman Louis B. Anderson's co-ownership is significant if corroborated. Needs directory/Defender verification.

entities.name: Royal Gardens / Lincoln Gardens
entities.summary: 31st Street jazz venue with documented Black ownership interests (1918-1921): Louis B. Anderson, William Bottoms, Virgil Williams (1918); Florence Majors (1921). King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band played there 1923-24.

claims.claim: Opened 1919 with 1,300 seats at 3143-3149 S. State; demolished 1949; Louis Armstrong performed there with Erskine Tate's Vendome Theater Symphony Orchestra in 1925; Fats Waller was house organist in 1927.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation; UChicago exhibition text documents Armstrong/Tate (1926) and Waller (1927).
claims.source: Bo Lindstrom (2012); UChicago Library exhibition text (1996-97)
claims.uncertainty: Demolition year 1949 rests on one compilation; ownership not verified.

entities.name: Vendome Theater
entities.summary: 1,300-seat State Street theater; Louis Armstrong performed there with Erskine Tate's orchestra in 1925; Fats Waller was house organist in 1927.

claims.claim: Operated circa 1908-1930 at 3104-3112 S. State; hosted the Original Creole Jazz Band (1913), Ma Rainey, and Bessie Smith.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation.
claims.uncertainty: Single source; ownership and exact dates unverified.

entities.name: Grand Theater
entities.summary: State Street Black-audience theater; hosted the Original Creole Jazz Band (1913), Ma Rainey, and Bessie Smith.

claims.claim: Opened 1916 at 3436-3440 S. State with 383 seats; Lovie Austin was musical director 1923-28.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation.
claims.uncertainty: Single source; ownership and operating dates unverified.

entities.name: Monogram Theatre
entities.summary: 383-seat State Street theater with Lovie Austin as musical director 1923-28.

claims.claim: The Lincoln Theatre stood at 3132 S. State; it was demolished and its site is now part of IIT.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation.
claims.uncertainty: Dates and ownership unresolved.

entities.dates_active: unknown; demolished; site now part of IIT
entities.name: Lincoln Theatre
entities.summary: State Street theater, demolished; the site is now part of the Illinois Institute of Technology campus.

claims.claim: 700-seat theater at 3505-3509 S. State, part of the Panama/De Luxe/States corner grouping.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation.
claims.uncertainty: Ownership and exact operating dates unverified.

entities.name: States Theater
entities.summary: 700-seat Black theater at the Panama (3501) / De Luxe Cafe (3503) / States corner cluster; described as one of the most prominent Black theaters in Chicago's Black Belt.

entities.address: 3501 S. State Street, Chicago (southeast corner, State and 35th)

claims.claim: The Panama Cafe at the southeast corner of State and 35th was white-owned; Florence Mills got her start there and Tony Jackson's 'Pretty Baby' dates to 1916 there.
claims.evidence: The NPS nomination explicitly verifies the Panama's white ownership and State/35th location; Lindstrom lists 3501 S. State, ca. 1910s-1920.
claims.source: NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985); Bo Lindstrom (2012)
claims.uncertainty: White ownership verified by NPS; the named white owner was not identified (gap). Performer details provisional.

entities.name: Panama Cafe (Panama Club)
entities.summary: White-owned early jazz incubator; Florence Mills got her start there; Tony Jackson's 'Pretty Baby' dates to 1916 there.

claims.claim: Black-and-tan jazz club at 338 E. 35th, open 1924 into the 1930s; Joe 'King' Oliver with the Dixie Syncopators played February 1925-spring 1927; it was bombed and destroyed by fire in spring 1927, later moving to 5060 S. Michigan (1934).
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation.
claims.uncertainty: Single source; the bombing claim in particular needs Defender/police-record corroboration. Do not state the bombing as established fact.

entities.dates_active: 1924-1930s; destroyed by fire spring 1927; later moved to 5060 S. Michigan (1934)
entities.name: Plantation Cafe
entities.summary: 'Black and Tan' jazz club; Joe 'King' Oliver played there February 1925-spring 1927.

claims.claim: Gerri's Palm Tavern at 446 E. 47th Street opened in 1933 and was locked/closed in 2001 after city acquisition.
claims.evidence: MAS Context preservation journalism documents the address, 1933 opening, and 2001 closure.
claims.source: MAS Context, 'What Happened to Gerri's Palm Tavern'
claims.uncertainty: Single source; demolition date and present site use unresolved. Important qualifier to the district-level white-ownership pattern of 47th Street.

entities.name: Palm Tavern (Gerri's Palm Tavern)
entities.summary: Documented Black-owned business on the 47th Street corridor; operated nearly 70 years; closed/locked 2001 after the city acquired the property.

entities.address: 330 E. 35th Street (also reported on Prairie Avenue)

claims.claim: A venue at 330 E. 35th operated as the Club Alvadere (1920-22), the Nest Club (ca. 1922-26), and the Apex Club (1926-28).
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation.
claims.uncertainty: Single source.

claims.claim: Address is disputed (330 E. 35th vs. Prairie Avenue — the UChicago exhibit documents 'Earl Hines with Jimmie Noone at an Apex Club on Prairie Avenue in 1928') and closure is disputed (1928 end of listing vs. 1930 federal Prohibition raid reported by a weak marketplace listing).
claims.evidence: Lindstrom vs. UChicago exhibition text; picclick listing.
claims.source: Bo Lindstrom (2012); UChicago Library exhibition text (1996-97)
claims.uncertainty: Do not state an address or closure date as fact without directory verification.

entities.name: Apex Club (formerly Nest Club; formerly Club Alvadere)
entities.summary: Successive 35th Street clubs; Earl Hines and Jimmie Noone associated with an Apex Club in 1928. Address and closure disputed.

claims.claim: Nightclub at 5521 S. State Street; operated 1934-1958; 1,000 seats.
claims.evidence: Alchetron mirror of Wikipedia infobox (tertiary/weak).
claims.uncertainty: Existence and importance are well attested (Queer Bronzeville series lists it among integrated venues), but address and dates rest on a single weak source. Do not publish the address without verification.

entities.name: Club DeLisa
entities.summary: Major Bronzeville nightclub; address and dates rest on a single weak source and should not be published without verification.

entities.address: State Street, South Side Chicago (reported boundaries vary: 26th-29th; 31st-35th; broadly 26th-39th)

claims.claim: 'The Stroll' designated the Black entertainment strip on State Street, but reported boundaries vary: an IIT finding aid gives 31st to 35th; a tour source gives 26th-29th; a music-history article describes successive 'strolls' at 31st and State (1920s), 47th and Garfield/55th (1930s-40s), and 63rd in Woodlawn (later).
claims.evidence: IIT finding aid; chicagodetours; Beachwood Reporter music-history article; Schlabach, 'Along the Streets of Bronzeville' references the State Street 'Stroll' district.
claims.source: IIT Bronzeville History Booklet; Beachwood Reporter
claims.uncertainty: Treat 'The Stroll' as a loosely defined, era-shifting term rather than a fixed boundary until Drake & Cayton (1945) and Defender usage are consulted directly.

entities.name: The Stroll
entities.summary: The Black entertainment strip on State Street; boundaries contested and the term shifted over time to successive nightlife centers.

claims.claim: Built 1913 with community fundraising plus Julius Rosenwald (Sears, Roebuck) philanthropy; served Great Migration newcomers with job training, temporary housing, and recreation.
claims.evidence: Chicago History Museum (2023): building completed 1913, Rosenwald + community funds.
claims.uncertainty: One source (Track D) says 'opened 1914'; treat 1913/1914 as a minor discrepancy.

claims.claim: In September 1915 Carter G. Woodson convened the founding meeting of the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (ASNLH, now ASALH) at the YMCA; Negro History Week (February 7, 1926) was organized there — the direct origin of Black History Month.
claims.evidence: Chicago History Museum (2023): Woodson ASNLH founding meeting Sept. 1915 at the Y. Chicago Southsider (2026): Negro History Week organized there Feb. 7, 1926.

claims.claim: In 1992 the Renaissance Collaborative (founded by Quinn Chapel AME and three other churches) was created to save the building; a ~$9M renovation in the late 1990s returned it to use; the building was closed in 1981 and had faced a demolition order in the mid-1990s.
claims.evidence: Track D: Roanoke Times 1996 (demolition-order fight); Wikipedia (renovation by TRC); EIN Presswire 2026 (TRC 'formed in 1992 to restore and preserve the Historic Former Wabash YMCA').
claims.uncertainty: TRC founding-year sources: primary-but-interested (org PR).

claims.claim: Listed in the NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985); individually listed on the NRHP April 30, 1986; designated a Chicago Landmark September 9, 1998 as part of the Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District.
claims.evidence: NPS nomination; City of Chicago landmark address list.
claims.source: NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985); City of Chicago landmark list

entities.name: Wabash Avenue YMCA
entities.summary: Black Metropolis-era social institution and Great Migration hub; birthplace of the ASNLH (1915) and Negro History Week (1926); saved from demolition by the Renaissance Collaborative.

entities.address: 3533 S. Giles Avenue (reported 3517-33 S. Giles in Track E), Chicago

claims.claim: Armory of the Black 8th Infantry Regiment ('Fighting 8th'); the first U.S. armory built for an African-American regiment.
claims.evidence: VT/Roanoke Times (1996); Wikipedia; listed in the NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination.
claims.source: Roanoke Times (1996); NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985)
claims.uncertainty: Regimental history not independently verified here; needs National Register records.

claims.claim: Listed on the NRHP April 30, 1986; designated a Chicago Landmark September 9, 1998; threatened with demolition (1996 reporting) and reopened in 1999 as the Chicago Military Academy at Bronzeville public high school.
claims.evidence: NPS nomination; City landmark list; Wikipedia (citing Public Building Commission of Chicago); Roanoke Times 1996 (threat); DVIDS/Illinois National Guard 2019 (current use).
claims.source: NPS (1985); City of Chicago landmark list; DVIDS (2019)
claims.uncertainty: The actor behind the 1996 demolition threat is cut off in the archived Roanoke Times text (gap).

entities.name: Eighth Regiment Armory
entities.summary: First U.S. armory built for an African-American regiment (the WWI 'Fighting 8th'); adaptively reused as the Chicago Military Academy at Bronzeville.

claims.claim: Built 1887 by L.B. Dixon for the Jewish Lakeside Club; Oscar Stanton De Priest established the People's Movement Club there in 1917; later William Dawson's political HQ; church use from the 1950s.
claims.evidence: Lindstrom compilation; Track D: Wikipedia/preservation sources.
claims.uncertainty: Single-source chain; De Priest's precise offices need proper sourcing.

claims.claim: Listed on the NRHP April 30, 1986; designated a Chicago Landmark September 9, 1998; vacant and endangered (WBEZ/Lee Bey, 2012). Current 2026 condition unverified.
claims.evidence: NPS nomination; City landmark list; WBEZ (April 2012).
claims.source: NPS (1985); City of Chicago landmark list; WBEZ (2012)
claims.uncertainty: Student-housing conversion plans unverified; needs a fresh condition check.

entities.name: Unity Hall
entities.summary: 1887 clubhouse; De Priest's 1917 political base; now vacant and endangered despite landmark protections.

claims.claim: Commissioned 1922 by Anthony Overton; architect Z. Erol Smith; completed 1923; housed Overton's conglomerate (Overton Hygienic Manufacturing Co., Victory Life, Douglass National Bank).
claims.evidence: NPS nomination identifies the surviving building; Next City (2019) and academic article document the enterprises; commissioning 1922 vs. completion 1923 treated as consistent.
claims.source: NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985); Next City (2019)
claims.uncertainty: Build-year specifics (1922 vs. completed 1923) minor.

claims.claim: Listed on the NRHP April 30, 1986; designated a Chicago Landmark September 9, 1998; renovated 2007 by the Davis Group ($8M financing stack), sparing it from potential demolition; being fitted as incubator space (~2019).
claims.evidence: NPS nomination; City landmark list; NextCity (~2019).
claims.source: NPS (1985); City of Chicago landmark list; NextCity (2019)
claims.uncertainty: Dollar figure as reported in a single detailed source; current occupancy unresolved.

entities.name: Overton Hygienic Building
entities.summary: Anthony Overton's corporate headquarters building, housing his cosmetics company, insurance company, and Douglass National Bank; landmarked and renovated in 2007.

claims.claim: Commissioned 1929 by Anthony Overton; completed 1931; housed the Chicago Bee newspaper; Art Deco building; now houses a Chicago Public Library branch (since 1996; reopened December 2018 after a $2.32M renovation funded by the Chicago Housing Authority).
claims.evidence: NPS nomination; Chicago Literary Hall of Fame; Preservation Chicago (2018); Citizen Newspaper Group (Dec 2018); do312 walking-tour listing.
claims.source: NPS (1985); Chicago Literary Hall of Fame; Preservation Chicago (2018)

claims.claim: Founded September 1916 out of the Union Grove Prayer Meeting Club (met in Deacon John A. Finnie's home at 242 E. 42nd St.; name suggested by Mrs. Finnie; first pastor Rev. Jessie D. Luck, Jan 1917); in 1922 purchased the former Kehilath Anshe Ma'ariv synagogue (built 1890-91; designed by Louis Sullivan and Dankmar Adler; initial drawings by draftsman Frank Lloyd Wright). (congregation's claim; NMAAHC catalogs 1922)
claims.evidence: Congressional Record, Sept 10, 2013 (Rep. Danny K. Davis tribute); Preservation Research Office (2006).

claims.uncertainty: 'Birthplace of gospel music' is a contested honorific with Ebenezer Missionary Baptist; use attributed language. claims.claim: NRHP 1973; Chicago Landmark 1981; Bessie Coleman was a member; hosted boxer Jack Johnson's funeral (1946); Martin Luther King Jr. preached there.
claims.evidence: Landmark records; secondary sources.

claims.claim: Devastating fire January 6, 2006 (roofers using a propane torch); only exterior walls survived; August 2020 storm collapsed the south wall; rebuilding stalled; sold 2017 to the National Museum of Gospel Music; ~$2.1M in state funds secured (~2022) toward the museum.

claims.uncertainty: Status of the $2.1M state grant and any construction as of 2026 unverified (gap).

entities.name: Pilgrim Baptist Church
entities.summary: Founded 1916; birthplace of modern gospel music (Dorsey, 1931); gutted by fire in 2006; rebuilding and National Museum of Gospel Music plans incomplete.

claims.claim: Formed 1902; in 1921 purchased the former Isaiah Temple (built 1898/1899 — described as Dankmar Adler's last design; a Classical Revival synagogue, the first Chicago synagogue with an attached school building).
claims.evidence: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report (June 2, 2011); NPS NRHP nomination form (2016, prepared by church trustee Patricia Butts).
claims.source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report (2011-06-02); NPS nomination (2016)
claims.uncertainty: Building date 1898 vs. 1899 varies by source; immaterial.

claims.claim: Thomas A. Dorsey organized his first modern gospel choir here in 1931, working with Theodore R. Frye and Roberta Martin; launched the careers of Sallie Martin ('Mother of Gospel'), Mahalia Jackson, and Dinah Washington. Also called 'the birthplace of gospel music' (contested with Pilgrim).
claims.evidence: City landmark report; NPS nomination.
claims.source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report (2011-06-02)
claims.uncertainty: 'Birthplace of gospel music' contested with Pilgrim; the Dorsey timeline (Ebenezer 1931 first, then Pilgrim 1931) lets both claims coexist if phrased carefully.

entities.name: Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church
entities.summary: Formed 1902; Dorsey organized his first gospel choir here in 1931; co-claimant of the 'birthplace of gospel music' honorific.

claims.claim: Founded 1919 (1918/1919 — church's centennial math supports 1918-1919); originated 1917 as the Olive Leaf Club, a religious social club formed by two South Side women, Mrs. Bertie Boone and Mrs. Maggie Walker, at 3732 S. Federal St.; first pastor Rev. D.W. Bowen; began as a storefront church.
claims.evidence: Church's own history page; Lynn Becker, 'Dr. King and the Story of Liberty Baptist Church'; Middlebury College archive (Rev. A.P. Jackson interview, Jan 3, 1992).

claims.claim: In 1924 purchased the Olivet Building (designed by Black architect J.M. entities.name: Liberty Baptist Church
entities.summary: Founded from a 1917 women's social club; built its own modern church (1952); MLK Jr.'s Chicago headquarters during the Chicago Freedom Movement.

entities.summary: Chicago's third Black Catholic parish (1933); provisional single-source finding.

entities.name: Jean Baptiste Point DuSable High School
entities.summary: Opened February 1935; one of Chicago's first two all-Black high schools; Chicago Landmark 2013.

entities.summary: New York Life's 1,640-unit urban-renewal redevelopment; displaced thousands of Black residents from 100+ cleared acres.

entities.name: South Side Community Art Center
entities.summary: Founded 1940; the country's oldest independently-run, continuously-operating Black arts institution; Chicago Landmark 1994; NRHP 2018; $15M expansion underway.

entities.summary: 1963 Perkins & Will school; NRHP-listed 2016; purchased 2015 and being converted to a creative-entrepreneurship incubator and community arts center.

claims.claim: 1929 Julius Rosenwald-funded apartment complex; CHA-owned; fell into despair, closed 2000; residents advocated ~two decades; Landmarks Illinois Most Endangered 2002; National Trust 11 Most Endangered 2003; saved and renovated into a $132M mixed-use affordable housing development (2016); ground-floor tenants include Sip & Savor and Shawn Michelle's Homemade Ice Cream; Ald. entities.summary: 1929 Rosenwald-funded apartments; closed 2000; saved through a ~two-decade resident campaign and rebuilt as $132M mixed-use affordable housing in 2016.

claims.source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City (2019)
claims.uncertainty: Brookings (2021) stated 'the nation's first Black-owned bank' — an upgrade of the regional claim; do not repeat the Brookings formulation.

claims.uncertainty: Needs landmark-record verification; Binga Arcade demolition date unresolved.

entities.name: Binga Bank / Binga State Bank
entities.summary: Jesse Binga's bank: private 1908, state charter 1921, collapsed June 1930; the first Black-owned bank in the Northern U.S.

claims.uncertainty: Confirm charter date from Comptroller of the Currency records or contemporary Defender coverage.

entities.name: Douglass National Bank
entities.summary: Anthony Overton's nationally chartered Black-owned bank (the second nationally chartered Black-owned bank in the U.S.); failed 1932.

entities.name: Supreme Life Insurance Company (originally Liberty Life Insurance Company)

entities.name: Chicago Defender
entities.summary: Founded 1905 by Robert S. Abbott; the nation's most widely circulated and influential Black weekly; a driver of the Great Migration.

entities.address: 3647-3655 S. State Street (Chicago Bee Building, completed 1931)

claims.claim: The Chicago Bee newspaper was founded by Anthony Overton in 1925 (Wikipedia/Next City) or 1926 (Clio/Chicago Literary Hall of Fame — Disputed: 1925 vs. 1926); staffed largely by women during its 20 years of operation; folded 1947, a year after Overton's death (July 3, 1946).
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Anthony Overton); Next City (2019); Clio; Chicago Literary Hall of Fame.
claims.source: Next City (2019); Clio; Chicago Literary Hall of Fame
claims.uncertainty: Founding year 1925 vs. 1926 disputed; the women-staffed claim is Provisional.

claims.claim: A Bee editor (theater editor James J. Gentry) coined the term 'Bronzeville'; the Bee sponsored the first 'Mayor of Bronzeville' contest — a circulation promotion, not an organic community coinage.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago (Gentry coined the word; the Bee's failed 1930 contest; Gentry carried the idea to the Defender's Robert Abbott in 1932; Charles Browning developed it into the Defender's 'second most profitable promotion').
claims.uncertainty: Some sources hedge to 'the 1930s' or attribute the name to the Defender alone (weak). An alternate account credits Alderman Louis B. Anderson's 1922 house (3800 S. Calumet) which he named 'Bronzeville.' Corpus position 2026-09-28: 1922 (Anderson house) vs 1930 (Gentry/Bee) origin theories both circulate; no primary source settles coinage. Do not publish Gentry-coinage as settled fact.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit harmonization 2026-09-28. H5: Verified -> Disputed. BVM-005's own red-team warned against simplistic coinage narratives; BCI-001 grades the origin Disputed.

entities.name: Chicago Bee
entities.summary: Anthony Overton's newspaper; a Bee editor coined the term 'Bronzeville' via a 1930 circulation-promotion contest.

claims.claim: Born 1865, Detroit; arrived in Chicago 1892/93; built a real-estate business serving Black migrants; founded Binga Bank (1908) and Binga State Bank (chartered 1921); opened the Arcade Building (1929); bank collapsed June 1930; convicted of embezzlement 1933 (Provisional); died June 13, 1950.

claims.source: NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985); BlackPast

entities.name: Frank L. Gillespie
entities.summary: Founder of Liberty Life Insurance Company (1919), later Supreme Life.

claims.evidence: ILGA House Resolution HR0406 (2003); Chicago landmark report.

entities.name: Robert Sengstacke Abbott
entities.summary: Founder of the Chicago Defender; his 1932 adoption of the 'Bronzeville' promotion (via the Defender's Charles Browning) popularized the name.

claims.claim: Born 1871 Alabama to formerly enslaved parents; moved to Chicago late 1880s; Cook County commissioner (1904-1908); Chicago's first Black alderman (1915-1917, 2nd Ward; acquitted of 1917 bribery indictment); 3rd Ward committeeman 1924; elected to Congress 1928 (seated April 15, 1929), first African American elected to Congress in the 20th century and first from a northern state; served three terms (1929-1935); lost seat to Arthur Mitchell (1934); alderman again 1943-1947; established the People's Movement Club at Unity Hall in 1917; lived at 4536-4538 S. King Drive (purchased 1929) until death May 1951 at Provident Hospital.
claims.evidence: NPS National Register nomination (De Priest apartment building); Illinois State University news (2021); Historical Marker Database; Lindstrom (Unity Hall).
claims.uncertainty: Minor date variance: 'elected 1928 / seated 1929' vs. 'served 1928-1935' — consistent.

entities.name: Oscar Stanton De Priest
entities.summary: Chicago's first Black alderman and the first African American elected to Congress in the 20th century (1929-1935).

claims.claim: First African American elected to Congress as a Democrat (1935-1943), defeating De Priest in 1934; born Lafayette, Alabama 1883; won Mitchell v. United States (1941) against Jim Crow rail accommodations.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; govinfo.gov (H.Doc. 108-224, Black Americans in Congress 1870-2007).

entities.name: Arthur Wergs Mitchell
entities.summary: First African American Democrat in Congress (1935-1943); defeated De Priest in 1934.

claims.claim: Succeeded Mitchell 1943 (served to 1970); first African American to chair a standing House committee — House Committee on Expenditures in the Executive Departments, January 18, 1949.
claims.evidence: Congressional Research Service RL30378 (congress.gov); H.Doc. 108-224.
claims.uncertainty: One Congressional Record tribute text mislabels Dawson '(R-IL)'; the CRS table correctly shows (D-IL).

entities.name: William Levi Dawson
entities.summary: Succeeded Mitchell in Congress (1943-1970); first African American to chair a standing House committee (1949).

claims.claim: Founded Provident Hospital and Training School in 1891 — the first African-American owned and operated (and first interracial) hospital in the U.S.; first nursing school for Black women in Chicago; performed an early successful pericardial/heart surgery there July 1893; hospital closed 1987, purchased by Cook County 1991, reopened 1993 as Provident Hospital of Cook County.
claims.evidence: Cook County Health FAQs (cookcountyhealth.org); Wikipedia.
claims.uncertainty: Priority dispute on the 1893 heart surgery (H.C. Dalton of St. Louis, 1891, cited by some sources) — noted, does not affect the institutional claim. Original first-12-bed-facility address not captured.

contradiction_noted.subject: Provident 'first Black-owned hospital in the U.S.' — Verified vs Provisional

entities.name: Dr. Daniel Hale Williams
entities.summary: Founder of Provident Hospital (1891), the first Black-owned and operated hospital in the U.S.

claims.claim: In September 1915 convened the founding meeting of the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (ASNLH, now ASALH) at the Wabash Avenue YMCA; Negro History Week (February 7, 1926) organized there — the direct origin of Black History Month.
claims.evidence: Chicago History Museum (2023); Chicago Southsider (2026).
claims.uncertainty: Woodson earned his Harvard Ph.D. in 1912 and attended the 1915 Lincoln Jubilee exposition in Chicago.

entities.name: Carter G. Woodson
entities.summary: Founder of the ASNLH (1915) at the Wabash YMCA; originator of Negro History Week (1926), the direct origin of Black History Month.

claims.claim: Lived at 3624 S. King Drive; co-founder of the NAACP (1909); anti-lynching journalist; house designated Chicago Landmark 1995; reported editor of the Chicago Bee during WWII (Provisional).

claims.uncertainty: Bee editorship Provisional.

entities.name: Ida B. Wells-Barnett
entities.summary: Anti-lynching journalist and NAACP co-founder; Bronzeville resident at 3624 S. King Drive.

claims.evidence: chicagoliteraryhof.org; pw.org; chicagoliteraryarchive.org; windycitytimes.com (2010).

entities.name: Gwendolyn Brooks

entities.name: Lorraine Hansberry
entities.summary: Playwright of 'A Raisin in the Sun' (1959); daughter of Hansberry v. Lee plaintiff Carl Augustus Hansberry.

claims.claim: Lived at 4831 S. Vincennes (Richard Wright House, landmark); wrote the original Introduction to 'Black Metropolis' (1945); Federal Writers' Project participant.
claims.evidence: windycitytimes.com (2010); publisher copy via Google Books.

entities.name: Richard Wright
entities.summary: Author; wrote the original Introduction to Drake & Cayton's 'Black Metropolis' (1945).

claims.claim: Performed at the Sunset Cafe (1926), the Dreamland Cafe, and the Vendome Theatre in Bronzeville; his Chicago residency was 1922-24 as a young musician (Dreamland/Sunset on the Stroll), not a Bronzeville lifetime.

entities.summary: Performed at the Sunset Cafe (1926), Dreamland Cafe, and Vendome Theatre; verify any residency claim against per-name sourcing.

entities.name: Nat King Cole
entities.summary: Attended Wendell Phillips Academy in Bronzeville (Provisional).

claims.uncertainty: Needs per-name sourcing.

entities.name: Bessie Coleman
entities.summary: First Black American woman pilot; Bronzeville resident in her early twenties (Provisional).

entities.summary: Historian and DuSable graduate (1937); chronicler of Great Migration Chicago via 'Bridges of Memory.'

entities.name: Vivian G. Harsh
entities.summary: Librarian and institution-builder; founder of the CPL's Special Negro Collection (now the Harsh Research Collection).

entities.summary: Clubwoman, historian, and settlement founder; historian of the Illinois Federation of Colored Women's Clubs.

entities.name: Irene McCoy Gaines
entities.summary: Social worker, clubwoman, and political organizer; her housing-committee work led to the Ida B. Wells Homes.

claims.uncertainty: Smithsonian exhibit detail Provisional pending direct confirmation. TikTok/SEO content farms inflate her story ('stolen wave') — cite only the Congressional Record facts.

entities.name: Marjorie Stewart Joyner
entities.summary: Inventor (permanent-wave machine, patent 1,693,515), beauty-industry executive, and civic leader.

claims.claim: Co-founded the Ebony Museum of Negro History and Art (1961), now the DuSable Museum of African American History; her 1955 ASNLH chapter fight with Irene McCoy Gaines shows Cold War ideological splits among Black women cultural workers.
claims.evidence: Peer-reviewed article cited above.
claims.uncertainty: Museum founding year widely repeated; verified via the scholarly article only for the 1955 episode.

entities.name: Margaret T.G. Burroughs
entities.summary: Artist and museum founder; co-founded the institution now known as the DuSable Museum (1961).

entities.name: Cora Carroll

entities.summary: First director of the Chicago Urban League.

claims.evidence: MIT Technology Review (2020); towardcommoncause.org; City Bureau (2024); Brookings (2022).

entities.name: Urban Juncture (Build Bronzeville)
entities.summary: Social enterprise founded 2003; rebuilds neighborhood commerce around culture and innovation.

claims.claim: Social-services nonprofit 'formed in 1992 to restore and preserve the Historic Former Wabash YMCA'; led the ~$9M late-1990s renovation; still operates from the building with community programming and the 2026 Black History Month exhibition partnership with the National Heritage Area.
claims.evidence: EIN Presswire (Feb 2026, org-adjacent PR); Wikipedia.
claims.uncertainty: Primary-but-interested PR; corroborated by renovation record.

entities.name: The Renaissance Collaborative
entities.summary: Nonprofit formed 1992 by Quinn Chapel AME and three other churches to restore the Wabash YMCA; still operates from the building.

claims.claim: Community organization that purchased the near-demolished Supreme Life Building in the 1990s and rehabilitated it (2005) as the Bronzeville Visitor Information Center; credited (NPR/WUOT) with saving and renovating 'several landmark buildings' alongside churches.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing Sun-Times 1996); WUOT/NPR (2022).
claims.uncertainty: Founding year and current operating status unknown (gap).

entities.name: Black Metropolis Convention and Tourism Council
entities.summary: Heritage-tourism organization; saved and rehabilitated the Supreme Life Building (2005). Founding year and current status unresolved.

claims.claim: Self-described focus: 'Community Economic Development with focus on information technology, heritage tourism, hospitality workforce development & training, preservation & sustainability' (Idealist); President Paula Robinson (~29 years as of ~2018); member of the GRIT Chicago development team for Bronzeville Lakefront.
claims.evidence: idealist.org (org self-description); Medill Reports Chicago (~2018); Chicago YIMBY (GRIT roster).
claims.uncertainty: Founding year unresolved (late-1980s per Robinson tenure — unconfirmed).

entities.name: Bronzeville Community Development Partnership
entities.summary: CDC focused on economic development, heritage tourism, and preservation; GRIT Chicago partner.

claims.claim: Formed in the early 1990s by community leaders including Harold Lucas Jr. (chairman Angelo Rose); Afrocentric planning vision; won city commitments of millions for infrastructure, landmark preservation, beautification; the $65M CPD headquarters; federal Empowerment Zone tax incentives.
claims.evidence: WUOT/NPR (Oct 2022, citing 1994 Tribune).
claims.uncertainty: Exact founding year and current status unresolved.

entities.name: Mid-South Planning and Development Commission
entities.summary: Early-1990s community planning commission with an Afrocentric vision; won major city commitments.

claims.claim: Founded 1916 (Middlebury says 1917 — minor variant) as a National Urban League affiliate by an interracial group of community leaders to aid Great Migration resettlement — employment, housing, adjustment to northern urban life; first director T. Arnold Hill (served until recalled to the national office in 1925); Arvarh Strickland's 'History of the Chicago Urban League' (U. Missouri Press) covers 1916-1960s.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; thefreelibrary.com (Eugene Kinckle Jones article); Strickland (U. Missouri Press, via bookseller copy).
claims.uncertainty: 1916 preponderant (Strickland's scholarly history dates it 1916); original headquarters address in Bronzeville unverified.

entities.name: Chicago Urban League
entities.summary: Founded 1916 to aid Great Migration resettlement; first director T. Arnold Hill.

claims.claim: The NAACP added its Chicago branch in 1912, among its first branches (with Boston). Christopher Robert Reed, 'The Chicago NAACP and the Rise of Black Professional Leadership, 1910-1966' (Indiana University Press, 1997), is the definitive scholarly history.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (NAACP); publisher copy (Reed, 1997).
claims.uncertainty: Widely repeated but Reed's book and NAACP records not directly consulted; branch headquarters location(s) in Bronzeville unverified.

entities.name: NAACP — Chicago Branch
entities.summary: Added 1912, among the NAACP's first branches. Branch headquarters location in Bronzeville unverified.

claims.claim: Congress passed the National Heritage Area Act in December 2022 (Senate unanimous; House 326-95); President Biden signed it January 5, 2023 (Public Law 117-339), establishing the Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area; up to $10M in federal funding over 15 years; covers 200+ locations between 18th and 71st Streets.
claims.evidence: Chicago Reporter (Dec 26, 2022); Sen. Duckworth press release; Wikipedia.
claims.uncertainty: Executive director as of 2026: Bernard Turner (EIN Presswire, primary-but-interested). Legislative prehistory: Rep. Bobby Rush's 2008 study act (never enacted); Sen. Durbin first introduced the Heritage Area Act in 2016.

entities.name: Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area
entities.summary: Federal heritage area established by Public Law 117-339 (January 5, 2023); up to $10M federal funding over 15 years; 200+ locations, 18th-71st Streets.

claims.claim: Designated a Chicago Landmark district September 9, 1998: Overton Hygienic Building, Chicago Bee Building, Wabash Avenue YMCA, Chicago Defender Building, Unity Hall, Eighth Regiment Armory, Sunset Cafe (listed by the city as 'Grand Terrace Cafe'), Victory Monument, Supreme Life Building. Six of the nine were individually listed on the NRHP April 30, 1986, as the 'Black Metropolis Thematic Resource' multiple-property submission (Overton Hygienic, Chicago Bee, Wabash YMCA, Unity Hall, Eighth Regiment Armory, Victory Monument). The district as a whole is NOT an NRHP-listed historic district.
claims.evidence: City of Chicago landmark address list (primary); NPS NRHP nomination (Form 10-900, primary); NextCity.
claims.source: City of Chicago landmark address list; NPS nomination (1985)
claims.uncertainty: A 1984 Commission on Chicago Landmarks consideration was rejected; a 1996 advocacy campaign preceded the 1998 designation (Roanoke Times, 1996).

entities.name: Black Metropolis-Bronzeville District (Chicago Landmark)
entities.summary: Nine-structure Chicago Landmark district designated September 9, 1998; six members individually NRHP-listed April 30, 1986.

claims.claim: 1927 agreement among white property owners in the Washington Park Subdivision (Woodlawn, immediately south of Bronzeville's historic core) barred sale/lease to African Americans; required owners of 95% of subdivision frontage to sign before taking effect; only 54% actually signed (filing certified 95%). Carl Augustus Hansberry purchased 6140 S. Rhodes Ave. in 1937, defying the covenant; Anna M. Lee (white homeowner, covenant signatory) sued.
claims.evidence: WikiLawSchool brief (95%/54% figures); Wikipedia; aggregatelitigation.com (Thomson Reuters case text, 2025); Mapping Inequality essay.

claims.claim: Prior action: Burke v. Kleiman (1934) — a class action in which Illinois courts held the covenant enforceable. In Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32 (1940), the U.S. Supreme Court reversed: res judicata could not bind defendants whose interests were not adequately represented (the 54% who supported the covenant could not represent the 46% opposed). Opinion by Justice Harlan F. Stone; argued by Earl B. Dickerson. The Court did NOT void restrictive covenants; that came with Shelley v. Kraemer (1948).
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; aggregatelitigation.com; Mapping Inequality essay.
claims.uncertainty: Decision date disputed: Nov 12, Nov 13, or Dec 12, 1940 (reporter citation 311 U.S. 32 and holding consistent). The geographic note: 6140 S. Rhodes is in Woodlawn, not Bronzeville proper — the case is central to Bronzeville's policy story (it cracked the covenant system confining Black Chicagoans to the Black Belt).

entities.name: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32 (1940)
entities.summary: Supreme Court reversal on res judicata grounds of a Woodlawn restrictive-covenant case; cracked but did not void the covenant system.

claims.claim: Chicago's HOLC residential-security map is dated 1940 (survey work late 1930s). Area D74 ran 'from 35th Street to 67th Street between State Street and Cottage Grove' and 'constituted the heart of the Black Belt, which included the Bronzeville and Washington Park neighborhoods' — graded D ('hazardous') with explicitly racialized descriptions ('the already negro-blighted district'; Washington Park 'almost completely monopolized by the colored race').
claims.evidence: Mapping Inequality Chicago context essay (quotes primary HOLC area descriptions); insurancenewsnet.com (2022, citing Treasurer Pappas study).
claims.uncertainty: Context page failed to reload on browser_open; evidence rests on crawled snippet. Map date 1940; survey work spanned late 1930s.

claims.claim: D-graded areas experienced worse long-run housing outcomes (Chicago Fed Aaronson-Hartley-Mazumder WP 2017-12); whether HOLC maps caused disinvestment vs. formalized pre-existing lender practice remains debated among scholars (Hillier 2003 vs. Aaronson et al.).
claims.evidence: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago working paper WP 2017-12; peer-reviewed literature.
claims.uncertainty: Causal weight: Verified as a research finding; direct causation vs. formalization debated.

entities.name: HOLC Residential Security Map — Chicago Area D74
entities.summary: 1940 HOLC map graded the Black Belt D ('hazardous') with explicitly racialized reasoning; long-run housing outcomes worse in D areas (Fed research), though causal weight is debated.

claims.claim: Named for the late Cook County Board president Dan Ryan Jr.; first segment (95th St to 71st St) opened December 12, 1961; full route (71st St to Eisenhower/I-290, plus Calumet Skyway connection) opened December 15, 1962, completing a $300M, 11.47-mile project; right-of-way clearance 1957-58; construction 1958 (first contract bids) / 1960-61.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia; chicagoroads.com; gribblenation.org; UIC oral history (Marshall Suloway transcript: clearance 1957-58).
claims.uncertainty: Clearance memory is participant recollection (one source) — Provisional on its own.

claims.claim: The route 'exactly parallels a historic black-white divide along Wentworth Avenue,' following the 11th/3rd ward border — heavily Irish Bridgeport to the west, predominantly Black Bronzeville/Grand Boulevard/Washington Park to the east (UChicago thesis, student scholarship — Provisional on the alignment claim); the 14-lane Dan Ryan bisected South Side communities (MPC 'Reconnecting Communities' report, Jan 2023; before/after maps). Displacement figures such as '12 square blocks and 10,000 residents' (TikTok) or '12,000 people' (video description) are Unresolved — no citable source.
claims.evidence: Theodosakis, UChicago thesis (knowledge.uchicago.edu); MPC report (metroplanning.org, Jan 2023).
claims.uncertainty: Bisection documented; decline-causation is interpretive. Arnold Hirsch, 'Making the Second Ghetto' (1983): the expressway corridor followed and hardened an existing racial boundary — an instrument of a larger racial-political project, not an exogenous shock.

entities.name: Dan Ryan Expressway
entities.summary: 14-lane expressway routed along the Black-white divide through/alongside Bronzeville's western edge; bisected South Side communities.

claims.claim: Federal and CHA policy placed the Wells Homes (1941) and the State Street Corridor towers incl. Robert Taylor Homes (1962) in/adjacent to Bronzeville; peak RTH occupancy ~27,000 vs. 11,000 designed. Plan for Transformation demolitions (1998-2011) coincide with the steepest 2000-2010 population drop.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Chicago; Wikipedia.
claims.uncertainty: Correlation to depopulation is Provisional (other drivers: outmigration after Shelley, deindustrialization, disinvestment). Hirsch (1983): CHA deliberately sited projects in the existing ghetto as a segregation device — the projects were a symptom of the racial order, not its cause.

entities.name: Public Housing Siting and Demolition (CHA Plan for Transformation)
entities.summary: Federal/CHA policy concentrated public housing in/adjacent to Bronzeville, then demolished it under HOPE VI/Plan for Transformation (1998-2011).

claims.claim: The Black-owned commercial core concentrated along east State Street between 35th and 39th (1908-1931, per NPS); the 47th Street district was principally developed and financed by white developers and store owners, with Black-owned/developed businesses largely excluded (NPS; Semmes 2006; City Black Renaissance report). During the Depression, white chain-store credit access helped 47th Street survive better than the Black-owned 35th/State district (NPS — Provisional on the causal credit-access mechanism).
claims.evidence: NPS Black Metropolis Thematic Nomination (1985); Semmes, 'The Regal Theater and Black Culture' (Palgrave, 2006); City of Chicago Black Renaissance Literary Movement Report.
claims.uncertainty: District-level pattern, not a claim that every 47th Street business was white-owned (e.g., Palm Tavern was Black-owned).

entities.name: Black Metropolis Commercial Geography (35th/State vs. 47th Street)
entities.summary: Black-owned commercial core on east State between 35th and 39th (1908-1931); the 47th Street district was principally white-developed and financed.

claims.claim: The Great Migration brought Black Southern migrants to Chicago; Bronzeville's population surged under segregation-era confinement (covenants, HOLC D-grading) into overcrowded kitchenette conversions; the combined Douglas + Grand Boulevard population peaked at 193,302 in 1950.
claims.evidence: Chicago Commission on Race Relations, 'The Negro in Chicago' (1922, primary); census series (Rob Paral compilation via Wikipedia — Provisional, needs NHGIS verification).
claims.source: Chicago Commission on Race Relations (1922); Rob Paral via Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Exact rent-premium figures (~20%/up to ~200%) encountered only via an unsourced video description — do not publish without verifying against the 1922 report. Census figures need direct Census/NHGIS verification.

entities.name: The Great Migration to Bronzeville
entities.summary: Southern Black migration to Chicago; Bronzeville's population peaked under segregation-era confinement in 1950.

claims.claim: Decline was multi-causal: deindustrialization + deliberate segregation policy (covenants to public-housing siting to expressway routing to urban renewal clearance) + demographic pressure + disinvestment, operating across the 1930s-1980s. No single villain; and 'decline' itself is partly a narrative artifact (Boyd 2008) — institutions persisted and people stayed.
claims.evidence: Hirsch (1983); Venkatesh (2000); Pattillo (2007); Manley et al. ('The Revanchist City'); Boyd (2008).
claims.uncertainty: The three single-cause stories (Dan Ryan killed Bronzeville; public housing destroyed the neighborhood; integration drained the middle class) are each misleading as single-cause accounts.

entities.name: Multi-Causal Decline Thesis (house position)
entities.summary: Bronzeville's post-1950 decline = deindustrialization + deliberate segregation policy + demographic pressure + disinvestment across 1930s-1980s; no single cause.

note: Grade normalization: Track A used a five-grade scale in which CORROBORATED meant two or more independent secondary sources in agreement. That maps to Verified under the master CTL four-grade vocabulary. Tracks B-F used the four-grade vocabulary directly. relationships.json contains only Verified-grade links.
